title: RecSoup: Efficient Model Merging Approach for Controllable Multi-Objective Recommendation
summary: Recommender systems often need to balance multiple conflicting objectives. Controllable Multi-Objective Recommendation (CMOR) enables dynamic adjustment of objective trade-offs at inference time without retraining, adapting to shifting user or system requirements. Existing CMOR approaches typically rely on output-level reranking or parameter-generating modules, which either limit the scope of feasible trade-offs or incur substantial training and inference cost. Model merging provides a promising alternative by reusing multiple objective-specific models via parameter combination. However, its direct application to recommender systems is challenging due to the lack of a shared linear regime and cross-objective interference. To address these issues, we propose RecSoup, a lightweight two-stage approach for effective CMOR via specialized model merging. RecSoup first mitigates parameter interference across objectives through a pruning strategy that jointly considers objective-specific importance and cross-objective relevance. It then performs adaptive parameter merging via a learnable preference-to-coefficient mapping, allowing dynamic trade-off control at inference time without joint retraining or additional generative modules. Theoretically, we prove that RecSoup outperforms the parameter generation paradigm in effectiveness and efficiency, as it can fully navigate the Pareto front without smoothness constraints. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that RecSoup achieves improved Pareto front quality and effective controllability while delivers 165--228x faster inference-time latency than parameter generation approaches. Code is available at https://github.com/35798642/RECSOUP.git.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes RecSoup, an efficient lightweight two-stage model merging approach for controllable multi-objective recommendation (CMOR), which solves existing CMOR's limitations of limited trade-off scope and high cost, and achieves better performance with much lower inference latency than prior methods.
AI.motivation: Controllable multi-objective recommendation needs to dynamically adjust objective trade-offs at inference without retraining to adapt to changing requirements. Existing CMOR methods either limit feasible trade-off ranges or have high training/inference costs. While model merging is a promising alternative that reuses objective-specific models via parameter combination, its direct application to recommendation suffers from lack of shared linear regime and cross-objective interference, which needs to be addressed.
AI.method: RecSoup is a lightweight two-stage model merging approach for CMOR. First, it applies a pruning strategy that considers both objective-specific parameter importance and cross-objective relevance to reduce cross-objective parameter interference. Second, it uses a learnable preference-to-coefficient mapping to achieve adaptive parameter merging, which supports dynamic trade-off control at inference without joint retraining or additional generative modules.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis proves RecSoup outperforms the parameter generation paradigm in both effectiveness and efficiency, and can fully explore the Pareto front without smoothness constraints. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks show RecSoup improves Pareto front quality and controllability, and delivers 165~228x faster inference latency than parameter generation methods.
AI.conclusion: RecSoup is an effective and efficient model merging approach for controllable multi-objective recommendation, which outperforms existing state-of-the-art CMOR methods in both performance and inference efficiency.

title: Architecting for Hardware Diversity: Meta's End-to-End Co-Design for High-Performance AI Training on AMD GPUs
summary: Meta deploys a heterogeneous fleet comprising NVIDIA GPUs, AMD GPUs, and proprietary MTIA accelerators to reduce costs and mitigate vendor lock-in. However, the extensive history of NVIDIA-specific optimizations hinders performance portability to other hardware. This paper presents our methods for optimizing alternative accelerators, using AMD Instinct MI350X versus NVIDIA B200 for recommendation model training as a case study. We propose three reusable principles. First, hardware-model co-design is essential: rather than directly porting models from NVIDIA GPUs, revising model structures and software recipes allows full exploitation of accelerator-specific strengths (e.g., MI350X's 1.6x HBM capacity relative to B200). Second, our analytical performance model enables zero-warmup optimal kernel selection across diverse datatypes and matrix shapes in production models, drastically simplifying tuning. Third, increasingly mature agentic workflows have lowered the barrier to porting from the CUDA ecosystem; we extend these workflows for microarchitecture-aware kernel optimizations and custom shim generation. Compared to the directly ported baseline, these methods deliver up to 1.5x improvement in end-to-end training throughput. To our knowledge, this is the first hyperscaler report on productionizing AMD GPUs for large-scale training. Our contributions have been upstreamed to the open-source PyTorch, Triton, and ROCm ecosystems.
comment: 16 pages, 21 figures, 6 tables. To appear in the 59th IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Microarchitecture (MICRO 2026)

AI.tldr: This paper describes Meta's end-to-end hardware-software co-design approach to productionize large-scale AI recommendation model training on AMD GPUs within a heterogeneous hardware fleet, delivering 1.5x throughput improvement over a naive ported baseline and contributing changes to open-source ecosystems.
AI.motivation: Meta uses a heterogeneous hardware fleet of NVIDIA GPUs, AMD GPUs, and custom MTIA accelerators to cut costs and avoid vendor lock-in, but existing NVIDIA-specific software optimizations prevent good performance portability to AMD hardware, creating a need for systematic optimization methods for alternative accelerators.
AI.method: The work uses AMD Instinct MI350X vs NVIDIA B200 for recommendation model training as a case study, and proposes three reusable principles: 1) hardware-model co-design that revises model structures and software recipes to leverage accelerator-specific strengths instead of direct porting; 2) an analytical performance model for zero-warmup optimal kernel selection across different datatypes and matrix shapes; 3) extending agentic workflows for microarchitecture-aware kernel optimization and custom shim generation to simplify porting from the CUDA ecosystem.
AI.result: The proposed methods deliver up to 1.5x improvement in end-to-end training throughput compared to the directly ported baseline. This work is the first report from a hyperscaler on productionizing AMD GPUs for large-scale training, and all contributions have been upstreamed to open-source PyTorch, Triton, and ROCm ecosystems.
AI.conclusion: The three proposed co-design and optimization principles are effective for porting and optimizing large-scale AI training workloads to alternative hardware, enabling good performance on AMD GPUs in Meta's heterogeneous production fleet, and the open-sourced contributions benefit the broader community.
AI.author_affiliations: All authors are affiliated with Meta Platforms, Inc.
AI.production_deployment: The paper claims this work is for real production deployment at Meta, and it is the first hyperscaler report on productionizing AMD GPUs for large-scale training.
AI.generative_recommendation: unclear. The paper focuses on recommendation model training but does not mention end-to-end generative recommendation as the core task or model architecture; it is about hardware performance optimization for general large recommendation model training, not centered on generative recommendation.
